tips.title: Transpiration is the loss, not the flow
tips.body: Transpiration is the **loss of water vapour from the leaves** through the stomata. The movement up the xylem is the **result**, and it is called the transpiration **stream**. Two words, two meanings: define the loss, then describe the stream it causes.

tips.title: Four factors, one mechanism each
tips.body: Light opens the stomata. Temperature gives molecules more energy. Wind **removes the humid air** around the leaf so the concentration gradient stays steep. Humidity does the opposite. Say the mechanism, not just the direction.

tips.title: Potometer measures uptake, not loss
tips.body: A potometer measures the water **taken up**, which is very close to but not the same as the water lost, since a little is used in photosynthesis. Saying so is a strong evaluation point.

tips.title: Say the mechanism for each factor
tips.body: Wind and humidity work through the **water vapour gradient** (wind removes humid air, humidity reduces the gradient). Temperature speeds up **evaporation and diffusion**. Light **opens the stomata**. Name the mechanism, then the direction.

why.matters:
Water goes up a tree with no pump anywhere in it, which takes some explaining. The answer is that water **evaporating from the leaves** pulls the whole column up behind it — the plant does not push, the sun pulls.

That gives the plant a permanent bargain to manage. The holes it opens to let carbon dioxide in are the holes water escapes from, so every minute of photosynthesis costs water. Most of what a plant does about its environment is a decision about that trade.

examples.title: Why a cut flower drinks
examples.body:
Put a cut stem in water and the level drops, with no roots and nothing alive below the cut. The pull is coming from the **top**: water evaporating out of the leaves drags the next molecule up behind it, and water molecules stick to each other well enough for the whole column to move.

That is what a **potometer** measures. It is worth knowing it measures water **uptake** rather than transpiration itself — most of what is taken up is lost from the leaves, but not quite all, and saying so is the difference between a good answer and a complete one.

visual.alt: A potometer: a cut shoot sealed into a tube of water with a capillary and an air bubble, whose movement measures how fast the shoot is taking water up

examples.title: The hole a plant cannot afford to leave open
examples.body:
A stoma is a gap between two **guard cells**, and it is the only way carbon dioxide gets in. It is also the way water gets out, so the plant is choosing between starving and drying every time it opens one.

Guard cells make the choice mechanically. Given water they swell, and because the inner wall is thicker than the outer they **curve apart** and the pore opens; short of water they go limp and it closes. That is also why most stomata are on the **underside** of a leaf, out of the sun and the wind.

visual.alt: A stoma between two guard cells, open when the guard cells are turgid and curve apart because their inner walls are thicker, and closed when they lose water and go flaccid

examples.title: Why washing dries fastest on the same day a plant wilts
examples.body:
Transpiration is evaporation followed by diffusion, so anything that speeds either of those up speeds the whole thing up — and it is exactly the weather that dries washing.

**Warm** gives the molecules more energy. **Windy** blows away the humid air sitting against the leaf, keeping the concentration difference steep. **Bright** opens the stomata for photosynthesis. Only **humidity** works the other way: damp air leaves less of a gradient to diffuse down. A hot windy day is a good drying day and a hard day to be a plant.

rows: blows away the humid air at the leaf

visual.alt: A table of the four factors affecting transpiration: light, temperature and wind all increase it, for their own reasons, while humidity is the one that decreases it by leaving less of a concentration difference

steps.title: The transpiration stream
steps.body:
Water evaporates from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells inside the leaf and diffuses out through the **stomata**. This loss is **transpiration**. As water leaves the top of the plant, more is pulled up the **xylem** to replace it, and more enters the roots by **osmosis**. The unbroken column of water moving from root to leaf is the **transpiration stream**. It is a passive process: the plant spends no energy on it.

The pore itself is the gap between two **guard cells**. When water flows into them they become **turgid**, bow apart and open the stoma; when water leaves they go **flaccid** and the stoma closes.

visuals.alt: Two stomata side by side: one open, with turgid guard cells, water vapour leaving and carbon dioxide entering, and one closed, with flaccid guard cells

check.prompt: Where does most water leave a plant?
check.solution: Stomata are the pores water vapour escapes through.

markScheme.description: Stomata

options: Through the bark of the stem
Through the root hair cells
Through the stomata in the leaves
Through the petals of the flowers

steps.title: Why plants need it
steps.body: Transpiration is a side effect of having stomata open for carbon dioxide, but the plant gets a lot from the stream of water it drives: water for **photosynthesis**, **mineral ions** carried up from the soil, **cooling** of the leaf as water evaporates, and cells kept **turgid** so the plant stays upright.

visuals.problem: A plant wilts on a hot afternoon. Explain why.

steps.text: Transpiration is fast in the heat, so water leaves the leaves quickly
The roots cannot supply water fast enough to replace it
Cells lose water and become flaccid, so the leaves droop

check.prompt: Which of these is carried up the plant in the transpiration stream?
check.solution: Mineral ions dissolve in the water taken in by the roots and travel up the xylem with it.

markScheme.description: Mineral ions

options: Amino acids made in the leaves
Dissolved sucrose
Grains of starch
Dissolved mineral ions

steps.title: What changes the rate
steps.body:
Transpiration is evaporation plus diffusion, so anything that speeds those up speeds up transpiration:

- **Light intensity**: stomata open in the light, so more water vapour can escape. In the dark they close and transpiration almost stops.
- **Temperature**: warmer water evaporates faster and molecules diffuse faster.
- **Air movement**: wind carries away the humid air next to the leaf, keeping the **concentration gradient** of water vapour steep.
- **Humidity**: moist air has a smaller gradient, so transpiration slows.

visuals.alt: Rate of transpiration against light intensity: rises as stomata open, then levels off once they are fully open

visuals.problem: Explain why transpiration is faster on a windy day.

steps.text: Water vapour diffuses out of the stomata and collects in the still air next to the leaf
Wind blows that humid air away
The gradient between inside and outside stays steep, so diffusion out is faster

check.prompt: Why does transpiration almost stop at night?
check.solution: No light, no photosynthesis, no need for open stomata.

markScheme.description: Stomata close

options: It is too cold for water to evaporate
The xylem empties at night
Plants respire only at night
The stomata close, so water vapour cannot escape

steps.title: Measuring it: the potometer
steps.body: A **potometer** measures how fast a leafy shoot takes up water. The shoot is cut **under water** so no air gets into the xylem, and the apparatus is sealed. As the shoot takes up water, an **air bubble** in the capillary tube moves along a scale. The **reservoir** tap resets the bubble for the next run.

visuals.alt: A potometer: a leafy shoot sealed into a tube, a capillary tube with a scale and an air bubble, and a reservoir with a tap

visuals.problem: Compare the rate with a fan on and off

steps.text: Set up the potometer and record where the bubble starts
Time how long the bubble takes to move a set distance, or how far it moves in one minute
Reset with the reservoir, switch the fan on, repeat
Keep light, temperature and the shoot the same; repeat three times and take a mean

check.prompt: What does the movement of the bubble in a potometer measure?
check.solution: The bubble follows the water drawn into the shoot. Uptake is a close stand-in for transpiration, not the same thing.

markScheme.description: Water uptake

options: The volume of water vapour lost by the leaves
The rate of photosynthesis
The volume of water taken up by the shoot
The number of open stomata

steps.title: Rate calculations
steps.body:
Rate is always **something per unit time**:

$$\text{rate} = \dfrac{\text{distance the bubble moves}}{\text{time}}$$

in mm per minute. To turn distance into a **volume** of water, use the capillary tube as a cylinder: volume $= \pi r^2 \times$ distance. Another method is to **weigh** a plant over a day: the loss of mass is water transpired, and percentage change $= \dfrac{\text{change}}{\text{original}} \times 100$.

visuals.problem: The bubble moves 36 mm in 4 minutes in a tube of radius 0.5 mm. Find the rate in mm per minute and in mm³ per minute.

steps.text: 36 ÷ 4 = 9 mm per minute
Volume per minute = π × 0.5² × 9 = π × 0.25 × 9 = 7.1 mm³ per minute
Always give the unit: mm per minute is not the same as mm³ per minute

check.prompt: The bubble moves 45 mm in 5 minutes. Calculate the rate in mm per minute.

steps.title: Translocation
steps.body: Sugar made in the leaves has to reach every other part of the plant. Dissolved **sucrose** is loaded into the **phloem** and carried to wherever it is needed: growing shoots and roots, developing fruits and seeds, and storage organs. This is **translocation**. The leaves are the **source**; the places that use or store sugar are **sinks**. It runs in **both directions**, and unlike transpiration it needs **energy**, supplied by the companion cells.

visuals.alt: Xylem carrying water upwards beside phloem carrying sucrose in both directions

check.solution: Water in xylem, sugar in phloem. Only translocation needs energy.

markScheme.description: Xylem water up; phloem sucrose both ways

options: Transpiration: phloem, sucrose, downwards. Translocation: xylem, water, upwards
Both need energy from the plant to move substances in either direction
Transpiration: xylem, water, upwards. Translocation: phloem, sucrose, both ways
Both use the xylem, moving water upwards and sucrose downwards

steps.title: Your turn: reading a potometer investigation
steps.body: A student records how far the bubble moves in 5 minutes under different conditions: still air 20 mm, fan 45 mm, plastic bag over the leaves 6 mm, lamp close 38 mm. Convert each to a rate, then explain each difference with evaporation or diffusion.

steps.text: Rate = 45 ÷ 5 = 9 mm per minute, against 4 mm per minute in still air
The fan removes humid air from around the leaves
The water vapour gradient stays steep, so diffusion out is faster
Lamp close: 38 ÷ 5 = 7.6 mm per minute. The light opens the stomata and warms the leaf, so evaporation and diffusion are both faster. Still air: 20 ÷ 5 = 4 mm per minute is the baseline.

check.prompt: With a plastic bag over the leaves the bubble moved 6 mm in 5 minutes. Calculate the rate in mm per minute.
check.solution: 6 ÷ 5 = 1.2 mm per minute. The bag traps humid air, so the gradient is small.

steps.title: Going deeper: evaluating the method
steps.body:
Top questions ask you to **evaluate** the potometer. Know its limits: it measures **uptake**, not transpiration, because a little water is used in photosynthesis or kept in the cells; an **air bubble in the xylem** stops it working, which is why the shoot is cut under water; and a cut shoot is not a whole plant with roots. Improvements are specific: seal joints with Vaseline, let the shoot settle before timing, repeat and average, keep every other factor constant.

The other grade 9 skill is **using data**: compare rates with numbers, then give the biology behind the difference: open stomata, faster evaporation and diffusion, or a steeper water vapour gradient.

visuals.problem: A student says "the potometer measures the rate of transpiration". Improve the statement.

steps.text: It measures the rate of water uptake by the shoot
Uptake is slightly greater than transpiration, because some water is used for photosynthesis and for keeping cells turgid
So uptake is a good estimate of transpiration, not the same quantity

check.prompt: A potometer reading is much lower than expected and the bubble hardly moves. Which is the most likely cause?
check.solution: A broken water column is the classic potometer failure.

markScheme.description: Air in the xylem

options: The reservoir was full, so water flowed the other way into the shoot
The leaves have too many stomata, so water is lost before it is measured
Air got into the xylem when the shoot was cut, breaking the water column
The fan was left on, which pushes the bubble backwards along the tube

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Transpiration: evaporation of water from the leaf surfaces and diffusion out through the stomata. It pulls the transpiration stream up the xylem; passive.
- Faster with more light (stomata open), higher temperature, and moving air; slower in humid air.
- Potometer: shoot cut under water, bubble moves along a scale. Rate = distance ÷ time; volume = πr² × distance.
- Translocation: sucrose in the phloem from source (leaves) to sinks, both directions, needs energy.
- Uptake is not quite transpiration: some water is used or kept.

questions.solution: Water evaporates from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells and diffuses out through the stomata.

questions.solution: Xylem. The column of water in it is pulled upwards as water evaporates from the leaves.

questions.prompt: Why does the rate of transpiration increase in bright light?
questions.solution: Stomata open to let carbon dioxide in. Water vapour leaves through the same pores.

markScheme.description: Stomata open

options: Light heats the water in the xylem so that it boils and escapes as steam
The stomata open in the light for photosynthesis, so more water vapour can escape
Light makes the leaves grow bigger, so there is more surface area for water to leave
The roots absorb more water in the light, so more is pushed out of the leaves

questions.prompt: In a potometer the air bubble moves 24 mm in 3 minutes. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm per minute. Type the number only.
questions.solution: Rate = distance ÷ time = 24 ÷ 3 = 8 mm per minute.

markScheme.description: 8 mm per minute

questions.prompt: Explain why moving air increases the rate of transpiration.
questions.solution: The key idea is the concentration gradient of water vapour between the inside of the leaf and the air outside.

markScheme.description: Water vapour builds up outside the leaf
Moving air removes it
Steeper gradient, faster diffusion

criteria.text: Water vapour collects in the air next to the leaf
Moving air removes it, keeping the air outside the leaf less humid
So the concentration gradient of water vapour between inside and outside the leaf stays steep, and diffusion out is faster

questions.modelAnswer: Water vapour diffuses out of the stomata and builds up in the still air next to the leaf, which makes the outside more humid. Moving air blows this water vapour away. That keeps the air outside the leaf drier than the air inside, so the concentration gradient stays steep and water vapour diffuses out faster.

questions.prompt: When setting up a potometer, the shoot is cut under water. Why?
questions.solution: An air bubble in the xylem breaks the column of water and stops uptake.

markScheme.description: Stops air entering the xylem

options: So that no air gets into the xylem and blocks the flow of water
So the shoot absorbs water through the cut end more quickly
So the leaves are washed clean
To keep the shoot cool

questions.prompt: A potometer has a capillary tube of radius 0.5 mm. The bubble moves 50 mm in 10 minutes. Calculate the volume of water taken up. Use volume = π × r² × distance. Give your answer in mm³ to 1 decimal place; type the number only.
questions.solution: Volume = π × 0.5² × 50 = π × 0.25 × 50 = 39.3 mm³ (3.93 mm³ per minute).

markScheme.description: 39.3 mm³

questions.prompt: Describe how water moves from the soil to the air around a plant.
questions.solution: Level-marked. Sequence matters: root, xylem, leaf, air, then the pull that connects them.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): one or two relevant points about the path of water and the transpiration pull, not linked
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): a mostly correct account of the path of water and the transpiration pull with some links
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a coherent, complete account of the path of water and the transpiration pull using the correct terms

criteria.text: Water enters root hair cells by osmosis, from the dilute soil water into the more concentrated cell contents
It passes across the root into the xylem
Water moves up the xylem in a continuous column, the transpiration stream
In the leaf, water evaporates from the surface of the mesophyll cells into the air spaces
Water vapour diffuses out through the stomata
Evaporation from the leaf pulls more water up the xylem to replace it, so the whole process is driven by transpiration

questions.modelAnswer: Water enters the root hair cells by osmosis, because the soil water is more dilute than the cell contents. It moves across the root and into the xylem. The xylem vessels form continuous hollow tubes, so the water rises as a single column, the transpiration stream, up the stem and into the leaf veins. In the leaf, water evaporates from the surfaces of the mesophyll cells into the air spaces, then diffuses out through the open stomata into the air. Because water is lost from the top, more is pulled up the xylem to replace it, and more enters at the roots. The pull of transpiration drives the whole movement.

questions.prompt: A potometer measures water uptake, not transpiration. Why are the two not exactly equal?
questions.solution: Uptake is slightly more than loss, because a little of the water stays in the plant or is used up.

markScheme.description: Some water used or retained

options: Water also leaves through the roots of the shoot, so the potometer misses the part that is lost below the cut end
Some of the water taken up is used in photosynthesis or kept in the cells to make them turgid, so not all of it is transpired
The bubble moves faster than the water, so the potometer always reads higher than the true rate of transpiration
The potometer measures the volume of the whole shoot, which changes as the leaves grow during the experiment

questions.prompt: Four similar leaves are hung up for two days. Leaf A has Vaseline on both surfaces, B on the upper surface only, C on the lower surface only, and D has none. Leaf A loses 2% of its mass, B loses 18%, C loses 5%, and D loses 20%. Explain these results.
questions.solution: Use the numbers: the comparison of B with C is the evidence.

markScheme.description: Vaseline blocks stomata
D most, A least
C loses much less than B
Most stomata on the lower surface

criteria.text: Vaseline blocks the stomata, so water vapour cannot escape through them
D loses most because both surfaces are open; A loses least because both are sealed
C (lower surface covered) loses much less than B (upper surface covered)
So most stomata are on the lower surface

questions.modelAnswer: Vaseline is waterproof and blocks the stomata, so water vapour cannot escape through the surface it covers. Leaf D, with nothing blocked, loses the most water, and leaf A, with both surfaces sealed, loses almost none. Leaf C, with only the lower surface sealed, loses far less than leaf B, with only the upper surface sealed. Sealing the lower surface makes the bigger difference, which shows that most of the stomata are on the lower surface of the leaf. The small loss from A and C comes from the cuticle and the cut stalk.

questions.prompt: A potted plant has a mass of 20.0 g at the start of a day and 18.4 g at the end. Calculate the percentage decrease in mass. Type the number only.
Translocation needs energy from respiration but transpiration does not. Why?
questions.solution: Loading sugar is an active process. The transpiration stream is powered by the evaporation of water from the leaves, which needs no energy from the plant.

markScheme.description: Active loading versus passive pull

options: Transpiration happens only at night when the plant is not respiring, so there is no energy available for it to use
Sugar molecules are heavier than water molecules, so they can only be moved upwards if the plant supplies energy to lift them
The phloem is much longer than the xylem, so sugar has further to travel and the plant must supply energy to push it the whole way
Sucrose is loaded into the phloem by active transport using energy from the companion cells; water is pulled up the xylem passively by evaporation

questions.prompt: In translocation, sucrose moves from a source to a sink. Name the main source of sucrose in a plant.
questions.solution: The leaves, where photosynthesis makes the sugar. Sinks are growing tips, roots, fruits and storage organs. A store such as a potato can become a source in spring.

markScheme.description: Leaves

questions.prompt: Why does the rate of transpiration increase on a warmer day?
questions.solution: Warmer water molecules have more energy, so **water evaporates faster and water vapour diffuses out of the leaf faster** through the stomata. Water in a plant does not boil, and if the stomata closed, transpiration would fall rather than rise.

markScheme.description: Water evaporates faster and water vapour diffuses out of the leaf faster

options: Water evaporates faster and water vapour diffuses out of the leaf faster
The stomata close in the heat, so water is pushed out through the cuticle
Water in the xylem boils, so steam escapes through the open stomata
The roots take in more water, so more is pushed out of the leaves

questions.prompt:
A student uses a potometer at four temperatures, keeping light and air movement the same. The table shows how far the air bubble moved in 5 minutes.

| Temperature (°C) | Distance moved in 5 minutes (mm) |
|---|---|
| 15 | 10 |
| 20 | 16 |
| 25 | 23 |
| 30 | 31 |

Calculate the rate of water uptake at 30 °C in mm per minute. Type the number only.
questions.solution: Rate = distance ÷ time = 31 ÷ 5 = **6.2 mm per minute**.

markScheme.description: 6.2 mm per minute

questions.prompt:
A student uses a potometer at four temperatures, keeping light and air movement the same. The table shows how far the air bubble moved in 5 minutes.

| Temperature (°C) | Distance moved in 5 minutes (mm) |
|---|---|
| 15 | 10 |
| 20 | 16 |
| 25 | 23 |
| 30 | 31 |

Which conclusion is best supported by these results?
questions.solution: Each higher temperature gave a longer distance in the same time (10, 16, 23 and 31 mm), so **the rate of water uptake increased at each higher temperature tested**. It did not double every 5 °C: 10 to 16 mm is × 1.6. A potometer measures uptake, not transpiration itself, and nothing was measured above 30 °C, so the trend cannot be stretched beyond it.

markScheme.description: The rate of water uptake increased at each higher temperature tested

options: The rate of water uptake doubled with every 5 °C rise in temperature
The potometer shows the exact rate of transpiration at each temperature
Transpiration would keep rising in the same way above 30 °C as well
The rate of water uptake increased at each higher temperature tested

questions.prompt: Which cells open and close the stomata in the surface of a leaf?
questions.solution: **Guard cells.** Each stoma is a pore between a pair of guard cells. When the guard cells take in water they swell and bend apart, so the pore opens; when they lose water they go limp and the pore closes. The stomata let carbon dioxide diffuse in for photosynthesis, and they are also where most of the water vapour leaves the plant in transpiration. Palisade cells are the photosynthesising cells inside the leaf, root hair cells absorb water from the soil, and xylem vessels carry water up the stem; none of them is part of a stoma.

markScheme.description: guard cells

options: Palisade cells
Guard cells
Root hair cells
Xylem vessels

questions.prompt: Mineral ions such as nitrate ions are absorbed by the roots and are needed in the leaves. How do they get there?
questions.skill: mineral ions in the transpiration stream
questions.solution: **Dissolved in the water moving up the xylem.** The mineral ions are taken into the root hair cells by active transport and dissolve in the water there. Water is drawn up the xylem by transpiration, the evaporation of water from the leaves, and the dissolved ions travel up with it, so the transpiration stream delivers both water and minerals to the leaves. The phloem carries sucrose, not the mineral ions coming up from the soil; ions in solution cannot diffuse up through air spaces; and the stem does not contain a pump of any kind, the pull comes from the leaves.

markScheme.description: dissolved in the water carried up the xylem by the transpiration stream

options: Carried up in the phloem by translocation, together with sucrose
Diffusing upwards through the air spaces inside the stem
Dissolved in the water that transpiration draws up the xylem
Pumped up the stem by muscle-like cells in the root

questions.prompt: In early spring a potato plant grows new shoots before it has any leaves, using sugars that were stored as starch in the potato tuber over winter. Which statement about translocation at this time is correct?
questions.skill: sources and sinks change with the season
questions.solution: **The tuber is now a source, and the growing shoots are sinks.** In translocation, sucrose moves in the phloem from a **source**, where it is made or released, to a **sink**, where it is used or stored. In summer the leaves are the source and the tuber is a sink, filling up with starch. In spring the roles reverse: the starch in the tuber is broken down to sucrose, which is loaded into the phloem and carried to the shoots, which need it for respiration and growth. So the phloem carries sucrose in either direction, depending on where the source and the sink are. Sucrose is not carried in the xylem, which transports water and mineral ions, and starch is insoluble, so it cannot be translocated at all; it is converted to sucrose first.

markScheme.description: the tuber is acting as a source and sucrose is carried in the phloem to the shoots, which are sinks

options: The tuber is acting as a sink, because sucrose in the phloem can only ever move from the leaves down to the storage organs
Sucrose is carried from the tuber to the shoots in the xylem, because the phloem does not work until the leaves have grown
The starch itself is translocated to the shoots in the phloem, and is broken down into sucrose when it arrives
The tuber is acting as a source, and sucrose is carried in the phloem to the growing shoots, which are sinks

questions.prompt: A student wants to compare the rate of transpiration of a holly shoot and a privet shoot. Each shoot is set up in turn in the same potometer, under the same light, temperature and air movement, and the rate of water uptake is recorded in mm³ per minute. The holly shoot has fewer, larger leaves than the privet shoot. Which change would make the comparison fair?
questions.solution: **Measure the leaf area of each shoot and express the rate per unit area.** Water leaves through the stomata, so a shoot with more leaf area has more stomata and takes up more water whatever species it is. The two shoots differ in leaf number and size, so a raw rate in mm³ per minute confounds the species with the amount of leaf. Dividing each rate by the total leaf area, for example by tracing the leaves onto squared paper, gives a rate per cm² that compares like with like. A wider capillary tube only makes the bubble move more slowly and does nothing about the difference between the shoots; letting the shoots dry out would make their stomata close and change the very thing being measured; and recording for longer does not alter a rate that is already per minute.

markScheme.description: measure the total leaf surface area of each shoot and give the rate per unit leaf area

options: Use a capillary tube with a wider bore, so the bubble moves more slowly and is easier to time
Let both shoots dry out for an hour before taking readings, so they start with the same water content
Record the holly shoot for twice as long as the privet shoot, because holly leaves have a thicker cuticle
Measure the total leaf surface area of each shoot and express the rate per cm² of leaf

questions.prompt: Name the tissue that carries dissolved sucrose from the leaves to the growing and storage parts of a plant.
questions.solution: **Phloem.** Sucrose made from the glucose of photosynthesis in the leaves is loaded into the phloem and carried to wherever it is needed: growing tips, roots, fruits and storage organs. This movement is **translocation**. Phloem is made of living cells, sieve tubes with companion cells beside them, and the transport uses energy from respiration. Xylem, the other transport tissue, carries water and mineral ions up from the roots and is made of dead, hollow cells.

markScheme.description: phloem

questions.prompt: A leafy shoot is set up in a potometer. At the start the air bubble is level with the 8 mm mark on the scale. Six minutes later it is level with the 50 mm mark. Calculate the rate of water uptake in mm per minute.
questions.skill: rate of uptake from two scale readings
questions.solution: Distance moved $= 50 - 8 = 42$ mm. Rate $= \dfrac{42}{6} = 7$ mm per minute. The bubble moves because water taken up by the shoot pulls the column of water along the capillary tube behind it, so the distance the bubble travels in a set time measures the rate of water **uptake**, which is close to, though not exactly the same as, the rate of transpiration.

markScheme.description: finds the distance moved, 50 − 8 = 42 mm, and divides by 6 minutes
7 mm per minute

questions.prompt: A student uses a potometer to compare water uptake by a leafy shoot in still air and in moving air, keeping the light intensity and temperature the same. In still air the bubble moves 36 mm in 12 minutes. With a fan blowing across the leaves it moves 90 mm in 10 minutes. The student says the moving air made the shoot take up water two and a half times as fast, because 90 is two and a half times 36. Calculate the actual percentage increase in the rate of water uptake caused by the moving air.
questions.skill: percentage increase in rate between two conditions
questions.solution: The two readings were taken over **different times**, so they must be turned into rates first. Still air: $\dfrac{36}{12} = 3$ mm per minute. Moving air: $\dfrac{90}{10} = 9$ mm per minute. The increase is $9 - 3 = 6$ mm per minute, and as a percentage of the original rate that is $\dfrac{6}{3} \times 100 = 200\%$. The rate tripled, not two and a half times: comparing the raw distances understated the effect because the moving-air reading was taken over a shorter time. Moving air sweeps away the water vapour that collects around the stomata, so the concentration gradient from the inside of the leaf to the outside stays steep and water vapour diffuses out faster.

markScheme.description: converts both readings to rates: 3 and 9 mm per minute
finds the increase and divides by the original rate (× 100): (9 − 3) ÷ 3 × 100

questions.prompt: Describe how guard cells open a stoma, and explain why the stomata of a plant close when the plant is short of water.
questions.solution: A stoma is a pore between two **guard cells**. When the guard cells **take in water** by osmosis they become **turgid** and swell. Their inner walls are thicker than their outer walls, so as they swell they **curve apart**, and the pore between them **opens**. When the plant is short of water the guard cells **lose water**, become **flaccid** and straighten, so the pore **closes**. This cuts the loss of water vapour by transpiration, which is what the plant needs when water is scarce, even though it also stops carbon dioxide getting in for photosynthesis.

markScheme.description: guard cells take in water (by osmosis) and become turgid or swell
the swollen guard cells curve apart, so the pore between them opens (thicker inner walls may be given as the reason)
when short of water the guard cells lose water, become flaccid and the stoma closes, reducing water loss by transpiration

criteria.text: Says that the guard cells take in water, by osmosis, and become turgid or swell
Describes the swollen guard cells bending or curving apart, so the pore between them opens (thicker inner walls may be given as the reason)
Explains that when the plant is short of water the guard cells lose water and become flaccid, so the stoma closes and less water is lost by transpiration

questions.modelAnswer: Each stoma is a pore between a pair of guard cells. When water moves into the guard cells by osmosis they become turgid and swell. The inner wall of each guard cell, next to the pore, is thicker than its outer wall, so the swelling cells bend outwards and curve away from each other, and the pore between them opens. This lets carbon dioxide diffuse into the leaf for photosynthesis, but it also lets water vapour diffuse out. When the plant is short of water, the guard cells lose water and become flaccid; they straighten and come together, so the stoma closes. Closing the stomata reduces the loss of water vapour by transpiration, which saves water when the roots cannot replace it, although it also slows photosynthesis because carbon dioxide can no longer get in.

questions.prompt: A student investigates the effect of light intensity on the rate of water uptake by a leafy shoot in a potometer, moving a lamp closer to the shoot for each reading. The rate rises as the lamp comes closer. Explain why the rate rises, and explain why placing a glass tank of water between the lamp and the shoot would make the student's conclusion more valid.
questions.skill: light, temperature and the control of variables
questions.solution: In brighter light more of the **stomata open**, so that carbon dioxide can diffuse in for photosynthesis. Open stomata also let **more water vapour diffuse out** of the leaf, so more water is drawn up the xylem to replace it and the bubble moves faster. The problem is that a lamp gives out **heat** as well as light. Each time it is brought closer the air and the leaves get **warmer**, and a higher temperature also raises the rate, because water evaporates faster inside the leaf. Two variables change at once, so the student cannot say how much of the increase is due to light. A tank of water between lamp and shoot **absorbs the heat** but lets the light through, so the temperature stays the same and only the light intensity changes.

markScheme.description: brighter light opens more stomata, so more water vapour diffuses out of the leaves and more water is drawn up to replace it
the lamp also warms the shoot, and a higher temperature raises the rate too, so two variables change at once and the rise cannot be attributed to light alone
the water absorbs the heat from the lamp but lets light through, so temperature is kept constant and only light intensity varies

criteria.text: Explains that in brighter light more stomata open, so more water vapour diffuses out of the leaves and more water is drawn up through the shoot to replace it
Explains that the lamp also heats the shoot, and a higher temperature increases the rate as well, so two variables are changing and the rise cannot be put down to light alone
Explains that the tank of water absorbs the heat from the lamp while letting the light through, so the temperature stays constant and only the light intensity is changed

questions.modelAnswer: The stomata open in the light so that carbon dioxide can diffuse into the leaf for photosynthesis. When the lamp is brought closer the light is more intense, more stomata open, and more water vapour diffuses out of the leaf through them. The water lost is replaced by water drawn up the xylem from the potometer, so the bubble moves further each minute and the measured rate of uptake rises. The difficulty is that a lamp is also a source of heat. Each time it is moved closer, the leaves and the air around them get warmer, and a higher temperature increases the rate of transpiration on its own, because water evaporates faster from the cells inside the leaf. Two variables, light intensity and temperature, are therefore changing together, and the student cannot tell how much of the rise is due to the light. A glass tank of water between the lamp and the shoot absorbs the heat from the lamp while letting the light pass through. The temperature at the shoot then stays constant whatever the distance of the lamp, so light intensity is the only variable being changed and the conclusion about its effect is valid.

questions.prompt: Compare transpiration and translocation. In your answer, refer to the substances moved, the tissues used and the structure of their cells, the direction of movement, and whether the plant has to supply energy from respiration.
questions.solution: **Substances.** Transpiration moves **water and dissolved mineral ions**; translocation moves **sucrose** in solution. **Tissue.** Transpiration uses the **xylem**, whose cells are **dead**, hollow tubes with walls strengthened by **lignin** and no end walls; translocation uses the **phloem**, whose **sieve tubes are living cells** with companion cells beside them. **Direction.** The transpiration stream goes **one way**, from the roots up to the leaves; translocation goes **from a source to a sink**, so sucrose can travel **up or down**, from the leaves to the roots in summer or from a storage organ to new shoots in spring. **Energy.** Transpiration is **passive**: the evaporation of water from the leaves pulls the column up, and the plant supplies no energy; translocation is **active** and uses **energy from respiration**, which is why the phloem must be alive. **Purpose.** Transpiration is largely a side effect of the stomata being open for gas exchange, though it delivers water and minerals and cools the leaf; translocation delivers the sugar made in photosynthesis to the cells that respire, grow or store it.

markScheme.description: Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): states one or two differences, such as water in the xylem and sucrose in the phloem, with little or no comparison of structure, direction or energy

Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): compares most of the points asked for, substances, tissues, direction and energy, but with a gap or a one-sided statement, such as naming the tissues without saying that xylem cells are dead and phloem cells living, or saying translocation needs energy without saying that transpiration does not

Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): a full comparison on every point: water and mineral ions against sucrose; dead lignified xylem vessels against living phloem sieve tubes; one way up against source to sink in either direction; passive movement driven by evaporation against active transport using energy from respiration; and links the energy difference to the cells being dead or alive

criteria.text: Compares the substances: transpiration moves water and dissolved mineral ions, translocation moves dissolved sucrose
Compares the tissues: xylem for transpiration, phloem for translocation
Compares the cells: xylem vessels are dead, hollow tubes strengthened with lignin, while phloem sieve tubes are living cells with companion cells
Compares the direction: the transpiration stream goes one way, from roots to leaves, while translocation goes from source to sink, so sucrose can move up or down the plant
Compares the energy: transpiration is passive, driven by evaporation from the leaves, while translocation uses energy from respiration
Links the energy difference to the cells: the phloem must be alive to respire and move sucrose, while dead, lignified xylem can carry a column pulled from above by evaporation

questions.modelAnswer:
**What is moved.** Transpiration moves **water**, with **mineral ions** dissolved in it, from the roots to the leaves. Translocation moves **sucrose**, the sugar the leaves make from the glucose of photosynthesis, dissolved in water.

**Which tissue, and what its cells are like.** Transpiration uses the **xylem**. Xylem vessels are **dead** cells joined end to end with their end walls gone, forming hollow tubes whose walls are strengthened with **lignin** so that they do not collapse under the pull. Translocation uses the **phloem**. Its sieve tubes are **living** cells, with perforated end walls, and each has a **companion cell** beside it that supplies much of the energy the sieve tube needs.

**Direction.** The transpiration stream runs **one way only**, from the roots up to the leaves, where the water evaporates. Translocation runs from a **source**, where sucrose is made or released, to a **sink**, where it is used or stored. In summer the leaves are the source and the roots, fruits and growing tips are sinks, so sucrose moves down and out; in spring a storage root or tuber becomes the source and the new shoots the sink, so it moves up. The phloem carries sucrose in **either direction**.

**Energy.** Transpiration is **passive**. Water evaporates from the cells of the leaf and diffuses out through the stomata, and this pulls the whole column of water up the xylem behind it; the sun supplies the energy and the plant supplies none, which is why the xylem can be dead. Translocation is **active**: loading sucrose into the phloem and moving it along uses **energy from respiration**, so the phloem has to be alive.

**Why each happens.** Transpiration is mostly a consequence of the stomata being open to let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis; the plant gains from it a supply of water for photosynthesis and support, a supply of mineral ions, and some cooling of the leaf. Translocation is the plant's delivery system, taking sugar from where it is made to every cell that respires it, grows with it or stores it as starch.

examTechnique.body: Transpiration questions are built around the potometer and the three factors named in the specification, plus humidity. Explain each factor by its own mechanism: light opens the stomata, temperature speeds up evaporation and diffusion, and wind and humidity change the water vapour concentration gradient. Give rates with a time in the unit. Evaluation marks come from knowing that the potometer measures uptake and what can go wrong with it.
examinerErrors: Saying transpiration is "water moving up the xylem". It is the loss of water vapour from the leaves; the movement up the xylem is the result.
Explaining wind as "blowing the water out of the leaf" instead of removing humid air to keep the gradient steep.
Giving a rate as a distance, with no time.
Saying the potometer measures transpiration directly.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer explains each factor by its own mechanism (open stomata, faster evaporation and diffusion, or the water vapour gradient), converts potometer readings into rates and volumes with correct units, uses the numbers when comparing conditions, and evaluates the potometer by naming what it really measures and where the method fails.
